rationale: A case traces visual hallucinations in the history of dementia with Lewy bodies and later catatonia during renal failure. The admission investigation concerns metabolic complications, medication and altered movement or responsiveness. It does not identify dried fig exposure or quantify visual hallucinations in relation to it.

The case uses polysomnography to distinguish persistent nightmares and REM-related motor phenomena from recurrent PTSD symptoms. The workup specifically reports absence of visual hallucinations and other neurological signs at assessment. There was no Parkinson fig exposure comparison.

The diagnostic study compares initial neuropsychological testing in autopsy-confirmed frontotemporal lobar degeneration and Alzheimer disease. A motor scale helps describe extrapyramidal features. The endpoints are cognitive testing and pathological classification rather than an ingredient or visual episode frequency.

A structural MRI study compares 25 people with Parkinson disease and current chronic visual hallucinations with 25 without hallucinations, matched for age and cognitive status. The authors assess visuoperceptive regions and separate cognition from hallucination group status. This comparison does not quantify a change in visual episode frequency after a documented food intake.

The case ultimately identified Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease with a progressive supranuclear palsy-like presentation. Visual hallucinations were reported during a levodopa trial before withdrawal of the drug. The original records the medication period and differential diagnosis without a measured food exposure or episode rate.

The study correlates striatal dopamine transporter imaging with resting-state connectivity in 23 drug-naive people with de novo Parkinson disease. Hallucinations appear in the rationale for differential dopaminergic effects reported elsewhere. The analysis does not test a fig exposure or a clinical visual hallucination endpoint.

The cross-sectional imaging comparison includes 46 people with Parkinson disease split by cognitive stage and 19 controls. The article notes quetiapine use in the dementia group for mild visual hallucinations. The measured comparisons concern metabolism and atrophy by cognition rather than visual episode frequency linked to food.

The PET study contrasts patterns of regional glucose metabolism and amyloid labeling in Lewy body dementia and Alzheimer disease. Hallucinations appear among the clinical features in the diagnosis and case table. The imaging comparison identifies no dried fig exposure or diet-linked symptom measure.

The 1984 retrospective series identifies 121 confirmed and 31 probable Creutzfeldt–Jakob cases, with possible diagnoses handled separately. In printed tables 4 and 5, visual hallucinations are recorded at presentation in 1% and during the subacute course in 17%. These are proportions of patients with the sign in a different disease and time window. The series supplies no dried fig exposure or Parkinson episode-rate estimate.
